# Scenario Analysis {#sec-965-scenario-analysis}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

What happens to a portfolio if yields rise by a hundred basis points, or if the
dollar appreciates by ten percent against every currency? A scenario is a
statement about a few factors, and the question is what it implies for every
asset that loads on them. @meucci2008 frames a scenario as a change of
probabilities on a panel of outcomes; @kupiec1998 places stress scenarios
inside the same distributional framework as value at risk, so that a scenario
has a probability and a loss rather than only a loss;
@breuer2009 ask which scenarios are at once plausible, severe and useful, and
answer with the worst loss inside an ellipsoid of plausible factor moves;
@glasserman2015 select scenarios by empirical likelihood; @rebonato2010 argues
that the factor moves of a scenario must be coherent with one another, which a
model of their joint behavior supplies and a list of shocks does not; and
@alexander2008 show how a market risk model supplies that coherence. Every one
of these starts from the same object: a mapping from factor moves to asset
returns. In the modeled market the mapping exists by construction, because
every series is the output of a factor model
(@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market), so a shock to a factor moves
every series that loads on it.

The generator itself is not shipped. What ships are the factor layers: the
level, slope and curvature of each region's curve and its two credit spreads in
`sim_curve_weekly`, the exchange rates in `sim_fx_weekly`, the five regional
equity classes and the commodity index. From them this appendix estimates a
mapping $\boldsymbol{B}$ from factor shocks to the return of every instrument
and every class, and then shocks it. Three things should be said plainly. The
mapping is estimated from the shipped data, by regression, and checked against
the analytical durations of @sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory where those
exist. It is linear and one-period: a scenario is a vector of simultaneous
factor moves, and the response is $\boldsymbol{B}$ times that vector. And it
is a tool for asking *what moves if*, not a re-run of the generator: the
idiosyncratic draws, the convexity of the bonds and the correlation between
factors are outside it, and @sec-965-scenario-analysis-episodes measures what
that costs by pushing the four episodes of `sim_episodes` through the mapping.

```{r}
#| label: data
A  <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_weekly, date, asset, return)   # 181 instruments, weekly
Rw <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_weekly, date, class, return)   # the sixteen classes, weekly
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)  # the same, monthly
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                 # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                      # excess returns
cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
fx <- sim_fx_weekly |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = date, names_from = region, values_from = fx_return) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
wk <- as.Date(zoo::index(A))
regions <- c("US", "UK", "EU", "CH", "JP"); foreign <- setdiff(regions, "US")
stopifnot(ncol(A) == nrow(sim_assets), ncol(Rw) == 16L, identical(zoo::index(Rw), zoo::index(A)),
          nrow(cv) == length(wk) + 1L, all(cv$date[-1] == wk), all(fx$date == wk),
          setequal(names(fx)[-1], foreign))
```

## Factor Exposures {#sec-965-scenario-analysis-exposures}

The factor set has thirty-five members. For each region there are the weekly
changes of the level, the slope and the curvature of its curve and of its
investment-grade and high-yield spreads; for each non-dollar region the return
of its currency; for each region the return of its equity market **in local
currency**, the class return less the currency's move by @eq-02-hedge, so that
the equity factor and the currency factor say different things; and the return
of the commodity index. The curve series are read in the units
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation established: the level, slope and
curvature are in percentage points and the spreads in decimals, so the first
three are divided by a hundred and a loading is a duration in years.

```{r}
#| label: factors
lsc <- grep("_(Level|Slope|Curvature)$", names(cv), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(max(abs(cv$US_Level)) > 1, max(cv$US_HY_Spread) < 1)   # percentage points; decimals
cv[lsc] <- cv[lsc] / 100
dcv <- as.data.frame(lapply(cv[-1], diff))                       # weekly changes, aligned with A
eq_local <- sapply(regions, function(rg)
  as.numeric(Rw[, paste0(rg, "_equity")]) - (if (rg == "US") 0 else fx[[rg]]))
colnames(eq_local) <- paste0(regions, "_equity")
ccy <- as.matrix(fx[foreign]); colnames(ccy) <- paste0(foreign, "_fx")
F <- cbind(as.matrix(dcv), ccy, eq_local, GLOBAL_commodity = as.numeric(Rw[, "GLOBAL_commodity"]))
stopifnot(nrow(F) == nrow(A), ncol(F) == 35L, !anyNA(F))
```

Which factors an instrument may load on is a design decision, not a search: a
government bond loads on its region's three curve factors, a credit bond also
on the spread of its grade, a money-market instrument on the curve, an equity
on its local market, a commodity on the commodity index, and every non-dollar
instrument on its currency. The sixteen class series are treated the same way,
except that a credit class loads on both spreads of its region. The exposures
are the coefficients of a regression of weekly returns on those factor changes,
with Newey–West standard errors as in @sec-05-factor-models-implementation
[@newey1987], and everything is indexed by name.

```{r}
#| label: exposures
meta <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  sim_assets |> dplyr::transmute(name = asset_id, region, kind = asset_class,
                                 grade = credit_grade, level = "instrument"),
  tibble::tibble(name = colnames(Rw), region = sub("_.*$", "", name),
                 kind = sub("^[^_]+_", "", name), grade = NA_character_, level = "class"))
factors_of <- function(region, kind, grade) {
  curve <- paste0(region, c("_Level", "_Slope", "_Curvature"))
  ccy   <- if (region %in% foreign) paste0(region, "_fx")
  spread <- if (is.na(grade)) paste0(region, c("_IG_Spread", "_HY_Spread")) else paste0(region, "_", grade, "_Spread")
  switch(kind, government = c(curve, ccy), money_market = c(curve, ccy),
         credit = c(curve, spread, ccy), equity = c(paste0(region, "_equity"), ccy),
         commodity = "GLOBAL_commodity")
}
expose <- function(y, cols) {
  m  <- stats::lm(y ~ ., data = data.frame(y = y, F[, cols, drop = FALSE]))
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  b  <- stats::coef(m)
  list(alpha = b[[1]], beta = b[-1], t = (b / sqrt(diag(nw)))[-1],
       r2 = suppressWarnings(summary(m)$r.squared))          # an identity row fits exactly
}
Y <- cbind(as.matrix(A), as.matrix(Rw))
stopifnot(identical(colnames(Y), meta$name))
fits <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(meta)),
               function(i) expose(Y[, i], factors_of(meta$region[i], meta$kind[i], meta$grade[i])))
B <- matrix(0, nrow(meta), ncol(F), dimnames = list(meta$name, colnames(F)))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(meta))) B[i, names(fits[[i]]$beta)] <- fits[[i]]$beta
alpha   <- setNames(vapply(fits, `[[`, numeric(1), "alpha"), meta$name)
meta$r2 <- vapply(fits, `[[`, numeric(1), "r2")
meta$t_first <- vapply(fits, function(f) f$t[[1]], numeric(1))   # level, market or commodity loading
stopifnot(all(abs(meta$t_first) > 5))

# An equally weighted class is the average of its instruments, so its row of B
# is the average of their rows. Asserted on the returns, not assumed.
members <- split(sim_assets$asset_id, paste0(sim_assets$region, "_", sim_assets$asset_class))
ew_classes <- grep("_(government|credit|commodity)$", colnames(Rw), value = TRUE)
stopifnot(all(ew_classes %in% names(members)),
          max(abs(as.matrix(Rw[, ew_classes]) -
                  sapply(members[ew_classes], function(ids) rowMeans(A[, ids])))) < 1e-8)
for (k in ew_classes) {
  B[k, ]     <- colMeans(B[members[[k]], , drop = FALSE])
  alpha[[k]] <- mean(alpha[members[[k]]])
}
```

For the bonds the exposures are known before any regression is run. A
zero-coupon bond of maturity $\tau$ has, by @eq-22-return, a loading of minus
its duration on the yield at its maturity, and the shipped factors are the
rotation of the two-, five- and ten-year yields that
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation identified, the observable level,
slope and curvature of @diebold2006: the level is the ten-year yield, the slope
the two-year less the ten-year, and the curvature twice the five-year less the
two ends. The loadings of the three yields on the three factors are therefore

```{r}
#| label: loadings
B_emp <- rbind(`2` = c(level = 1, slope = 1, curvature = 0),
               `5` = c(1, 0.5, 0.5), `10` = c(1, 0, 0))
B_emp
```

and the analytical exposure of a bond of maturity $\tau$ is $-D(\tau)$ times
its row, with $D(\tau) = \tau / (1 + \bar y(\tau))$ the modified duration under
annual compounding at the mean yield; a credit bond adds a spread duration of
the same size [@merton1974], and a non-dollar bond a loading of one on its
currency. The latent loadings of @nelson1987 at the Diebold–Li decay are a
different rotation of the same three yields, shown in
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation; the mapping uses the rotation the
data ship. The maturities are inferred as in that chapter, from the level
loading, and the regression is required to recover the analytical level loading
within ten percent.

```{r}
#| label: durations
bonds <- meta |>
  dplyr::filter(level == "instrument", kind %in% c("government", "credit")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(b_level = B[cbind(name, paste0(region, "_Level"))]) |>
  dplyr::group_by(region, kind, grade) |>
  dplyr::mutate(maturity = c(10, 5, 2)[rank(b_level)]) |>          # most negative: the ten-year
  dplyr::ungroup()
stopifnot(all(table(bonds$region, bonds$maturity) == 3L))
ybar <- function(rg, tau)                                            # mean yield at maturity tau
  mean(as.matrix(cv[, paste0(rg, c("_Level", "_Slope", "_Curvature"))]) %*% B_emp[as.character(tau), ])
bonds <- bonds |>
  dplyr::mutate(D = maturity / (1 + mapply(ybar, region, maturity)),
                a_level = -D * B_emp[as.character(maturity), "level"],
                a_slope = -D * B_emp[as.character(maturity), "slope"],
                a_curv  = -D * B_emp[as.character(maturity), "curvature"],
                a_spread = ifelse(kind == "credit", -D, NA_real_),
                b_slope = B[cbind(name, paste0(region, "_Slope"))],
                b_curv  = B[cbind(name, paste0(region, "_Curvature"))],
                b_spread = ifelse(kind == "credit",
                                  B[cbind(name, paste0(region, "_", ifelse(is.na(grade), "IG", grade), "_Spread"))],
                                  NA_real_))
stopifnot(all(abs(bonds$b_level / bonds$a_level - 1) < 0.10))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-965-bonds
#| tbl-cap: "The nine US bond instruments: analytical exposures (minus the modified duration times the loading of the bond's yield on each factor, and minus the duration on the spread) against the regression estimates, with the R² of the regression. A loading is in years; a spread or yield shock in decimals times a loading is a return."
#| echo: false
bonds |>
  dplyr::filter(region == "US") |>
  dplyr::arrange(kind != "government", grade, maturity) |>
  dplyr::transmute(name, grade = ifelse(is.na(grade), "", grade), maturity,
                   level = sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", a_level, b_level),
                   slope = sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", a_slope, b_slope),
                   curvature = sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", a_curv, b_curv),
                   spread = ifelse(is.na(a_spread), "", sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", a_spread, b_spread)),
                   r2 = sprintf("%.3f", r2)) |>
  kable(align = "llrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "grade", "maturity", "level", "slope", "curvature", "spread", "R²"))
```

```{r}
#| label: exposure-facts
#| include: false
r2_by <- meta |> dplyr::group_by(level, kind) |>
  dplyr::summarise(min = min(r2), median = median(r2), max = max(r2), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop")
r2_at <- function(lv, k, s) r2_by[[s]][r2_by$level == lv & r2_by$kind == k]
fx_load <- bonds |> dplyr::filter(region != "US") |>
  dplyr::mutate(b_fx = B[cbind(name, paste0(region, "_fx"))])
eq_beta <- meta |> dplyr::filter(level == "instrument", kind == "equity") |>
  dplyr::mutate(beta = B[cbind(name, paste0(region, "_equity"))])
dev_level <- max(abs(bonds$b_level / bonds$a_level - 1))
rho_sp <- sapply(regions, function(rg)
  stats::cor(dcv[[paste0(rg, "_IG_Spread")]], dcv[[paste0(rg, "_HY_Spread")]]))
dev_other <- max(abs(c(bonds$b_slope - bonds$a_slope, bonds$b_curv - bonds$a_curv,
                       bonds$b_spread - bonds$a_spread)), na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(dev_other < 2,
          r2_at("instrument", "government", "min") > 0.95,
          r2_at("instrument", "credit", "min") > 0.9,
          all(abs(fx_load$b_fx - 1) < 0.05),
          r2_at("instrument", "equity", "max") < 0.9,
          r2_at("class", "government", "min") > 0.99,
          r2_at("class", "credit", "min") > 0.99)
```

In @tbl-965-bonds the two columns agree within
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * dev_level)` percent on the level for every bond of
every region, and within `r sprintf("%.1f", dev_other)` years on the slope,
the curvature and the spread: the regression recovers the durations the theory
states, the near rank deficiency of @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory seen one
bond at a time. Across all `r r2_at("instrument", "government", "n")`
government and `r r2_at("instrument", "credit", "n")` credit instruments the
lowest $R^2$ is
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(r2_at("instrument", "government", "min"), r2_at("instrument", "credit", "min")))`,
and every non-dollar bond loads on its currency within five percent of one.
The `r r2_at("instrument", "equity", "n")` equities are the other extreme: a
median beta on the local market of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(eq_beta$beta))`
and a median $R^2$ of
`r sprintf("%.2f", r2_at("instrument", "equity", "median"))`, the rest being
the idiosyncratic draw that no factor carries (@fig-965-r2).

```{r}
#| label: fig-965-r2
#| fig-cap: "R² of the exposure regressions, one point per instrument and one per class series, by asset class. A bond is spanned by its curve, its spread and its currency; an equity is its market plus an idiosyncratic draw the mapping cannot carry."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.45
meta |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = factor(kind, c("government", "credit", "money_market", "equity", "commodity")),
                level = factor(level, c("instrument", "class"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(r2, kind, colour = level, shape = level)) +
  ggplot2::geom_jitter(height = 0.15, width = 0, size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "R² of the exposure regression", y = NULL)
```

At class level the rows of $\boldsymbol{B}$ are what a scenario needs, and
@tbl-965-classes collects them. The equity classes and the commodity index are
themselves factor layers, so their rows are identities by construction: a
foreign equity class is one times its local market plus one times its
currency. What the mapping adds is the bond block, where a class is an
equally weighted ladder of three maturities and its row is, by
@eq-22-exposure, the average of its instruments' rows, which the chunk above
asserts on the returns themselves. The credit rows are built that way for a
second reason: the two spreads of a region share one credit factor
(@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory), their weekly changes correlate at
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(rho_sp))` or more, and a regression of the class on
both cannot tell their loadings apart, whereas each credit instrument loads on
the spread of its own grade. The regression at class level is kept as the
check, and its $R^2$ is the last column.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-965-classes
#| tbl-cap: "Factor exposures of the sixteen class series. Level, slope, curvature and the two spreads are in years; currency, equity and commodity are return betas; blank where the class does not load on the factor. The R² is from the regression of the weekly class return on the region's factor changes."
#| echo: false
b_at <- function(nm, col) vapply(seq_along(nm), function(i)
  if (col[i] %in% colnames(B)) B[nm[i], col[i]] else NA_real_, numeric(1))
classes <- meta |>
  dplyr::filter(level == "class") |>
  dplyr::mutate(level_d = b_at(name, paste0(region, "_Level")),
                slope_d = b_at(name, paste0(region, "_Slope")),
                curv_d  = b_at(name, paste0(region, "_Curvature")),
                ig_d    = b_at(name, paste0(region, "_IG_Spread")),
                hy_d    = b_at(name, paste0(region, "_HY_Spread")),
                ccy_b   = b_at(name, paste0(region, "_fx")),
                eq_b    = b_at(name, paste0(region, "_equity")),
                cmd_b   = b_at(name, "GLOBAL_commodity")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(level_d:cmd_b), ~ ifelse(.x == 0, NA_real_, .x))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = factor(kind, c("government", "credit", "equity", "commodity")),
                region = factor(region, c("US", "UK", "EU", "CH", "JP", "GLOBAL"))) |>
  dplyr::arrange(kind, region)
stopifnot(nrow(classes) == 16L)
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(is.na(x), "", sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x))
classes |>
  dplyr::transmute(name, level = fmt(level_d), slope = fmt(slope_d), curvature = fmt(curv_d),
                   IG = fmt(ig_d), HY = fmt(hy_d), currency = fmt(ccy_b), equity = fmt(eq_b),
                   commodity = fmt(cmd_b), r2 = sprintf("%.3f", r2)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "level", "slope", "curvature", "IG", "HY", "currency", "equity", "commodity", "R²"))
```

## Shocks and Their Propagation {#sec-965-scenario-analysis-shocks}

A scenario is a named vector of factor shocks, zero wherever it is silent, and
its propagation is one matrix product,

$$
\boldsymbol{r}^{\text{scenario}} = \boldsymbol{B}\,\boldsymbol{s},
$$ {#eq-965-propagate}

with $\boldsymbol{s}$ the shock vector in the factors' own units: a yield or
spread change in decimals, a currency, equity or commodity move as a return.
The function refuses a shock whose names do not match the columns of
$\boldsymbol{B}$, for the reason @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation gives.

```{r}
#| label: propagate
shock <- function(...) {
  s <- setNames(rep(0, ncol(F)), colnames(F)); v <- c(...)
  stopifnot(all(names(v) %in% names(s)))
  s[names(v)] <- v; s
}
propagate <- function(shock, B) {
  stopifnot(identical(names(shock), colnames(B)))
  drop(B %*% shock)
}
scenarios <- list(
  "curves +100 bp" = shock(setNames(rep(0.01, 5), paste0(regions, "_Level"))),
  "spreads +200 bp, equities -15%" = shock(
    setNames(rep(0.02, 10), paste0(rep(regions, each = 2), c("_IG_Spread", "_HY_Spread"))),
    setNames(rep(-0.15, 5), paste0(regions, "_equity"))),
  "dollar +10%" = shock(setNames(rep(-0.10, 4), paste0(foreign, "_fx"))),
  "equities -25%, curves -50 bp" = shock(
    setNames(rep(-0.25, 5), paste0(regions, "_equity")),
    setNames(rep(-0.005, 5), paste0(regions, "_Level"))))
S_class <- sapply(scenarios, propagate, B = B[colnames(R), ])
stopifnot(identical(rownames(S_class), colnames(R)))
```

The four scenarios are a parallel rise of one hundred basis points in every
curve, which moves the level alone because the slope and the curvature are
differences of yields; a widening of every credit spread by two hundred basis
points with every equity market down fifteen percent in local currency; an
appreciation of the dollar that takes ten percent off the dollar value of every
other currency; and an equity sell-off of twenty-five percent with every curve
rallying fifty basis points. They are received by the policy portfolio of
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-application, recomputed as that chapter builds
it, a tangency portfolio across sleeves that are a tangency portfolio for
equity and minimum variance for government and credit, and by three strategies
of the register of @sec-25-backtesting-application at full-sample weights:
long-only minimum variance, long-only tangency and equal weight.

```{r}
#| label: portfolios
S <- stats::cov(Re); mu <- colMeans(Re)
sleeve_of <- function(a) ifelse(grepl("_equity$", a), "equity",
                         ifelse(grepl("_government$", a), "government",
                         ifelse(grepl("_credit$", a), "credit", "commodity")))
sleeves <- split(colnames(Re), sleeve_of(colnames(Re)))
qp <- function(S, mu = NULL) {                 # long-only minimum variance, or tangency given mu
  n <- ncol(S); a <- if (is.null(mu)) rep(1, n) else mu
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(2 * S, rep(0, n), cbind(a, diag(n)), c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  w <- pmax(sol$solution, 0); setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(S))
}
v <- list(commodity  = c(GLOBAL_commodity = 1),
          credit     = qp(S[sleeves$credit, sleeves$credit]),
          equity     = qp(S[sleeves$equity, sleeves$equity], mu[sleeves$equity]),
          government = qp(S[sleeves$government, sleeves$government]))[names(sleeves)]
sl <- sapply(names(v), function(k) as.numeric(Re[, names(v[[k]])] %*% v[[k]]))
b  <- qp(stats::cov(sl), colMeans(sl))
w_policy <- unlist(lapply(names(v), function(k) b[[k]] * v[[k]]))[colnames(Re)]

base  <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |> add.constraint(type = "long_only")
w_gmv <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, base |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                                           optimize_method = "ROI"))
w_tan <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, base |> add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
                                             add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev"),
                                           optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE))
W <- cbind(policy = w_policy, `minimum variance` = w_gmv[colnames(Re)],
           tangency = w_tan[colnames(Re)], `equal weight` = 1 / ncol(Re))
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W), colnames(R)), all(abs(colSums(W) - 1) < 1e-6), !anyNA(W))
round(W[rowSums(W > 0.005) > 0, ], 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-965-scenarios
#| tbl-cap: "The four scenarios propagated through the class-level mapping: the return of every class series and of four portfolios, the policy portfolio of chapter 15 and the register's strategies at full-sample weights."
#| echo: false
sc <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::as_tibble(S_class, rownames = "name") |> dplyr::mutate(kind = "class"),
  tibble::as_tibble(t(W) %*% S_class, rownames = "name") |> dplyr::mutate(kind = "portfolio")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(name, kind), names_to = "scenario", values_to = "ret") |>
  dplyr::mutate(scenario = factor(scenario, names(scenarios)),
                name = factor(name, c(classes$name, colnames(W))))
stopifnot(!anyNA(sc$name), nrow(sc) == 20L * 4L)
sc |>
  dplyr::arrange(name) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = name, names_from = scenario, values_from = ret) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-name, ~ sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * .x))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-965-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "The return of each class series under the four scenarios, from the linear mapping of @eq-965-propagate."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.8
sc |>
  dplyr::filter(kind == "class") |>
  dplyr::mutate(block = factor(sub("^[^_]+_", "", name), c("government", "credit", "equity", "commodity"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(ret, name, fill = block)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col() +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ scenario, ncol = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "scenario return", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: scenario-facts
#| include: false
pf  <- sc |> dplyr::filter(kind == "portfolio")
pf_at <- function(p, s) pf$ret[pf$name == p & pf$scenario == s]
cl  <- sc |> dplyr::filter(kind == "class")
cl_at <- function(c, s) cl$ret[cl$name == c & cl$scenario == s]
worst_of <- function(s) { x <- cl[cl$scenario == s, ]; as.character(x$name[which.min(x$ret)]) }
bond_cl <- grep("_(government|credit)$", colnames(R), value = TRUE)
us_cl   <- grep("^US_", colnames(R), value = TRUE)
rng <- function(s, cls) range(cl$ret[cl$scenario == s & cl$name %in% cls])
rank_of <- function(s) { x <- pf[pf$scenario == s, ]; setNames(rank(x$ret), x$name) }
r1 <- rank_of("curves +100 bp"); r2 <- rank_of("spreads +200 bp, equities -15%")
r3 <- rank_of("dollar +10%");    r4 <- rank_of("equities -25%, curves -50 bp")
stopifnot(r1[["minimum variance"]] == 1, r1[["equal weight"]] == 4,          # worst, best
          all(c(r2[["minimum variance"]], r3[["minimum variance"]], r4[["minimum variance"]]) == 4),
          all(c(r2[["equal weight"]], r3[["equal weight"]], r4[["equal weight"]]) == 1),
          all(abs(cl$ret[cl$scenario == "curves +100 bp" & cl$name %in% bond_cl] + 0.054) < 0.004),
          all(cl$ret[cl$scenario == "curves +100 bp" & !cl$name %in% bond_cl] == 0),
          all(cl$ret[cl$scenario == "dollar +10%" & cl$name %in% c(us_cl, "GLOBAL_commodity")] == 0),
          all(abs(cl$ret[cl$scenario == "dollar +10%" & !cl$name %in% c(us_cl, "GLOBAL_commodity")] + 0.10) < 1e-3),
          all(cl$ret[cl$scenario == "equities -25%, curves -50 bp" & cl$name %in% bond_cl] > 0),
          W["US_government", "minimum variance"] > 0.8)
```

@tbl-965-scenarios and @fig-965-scenarios read the mapping across the four
scenarios, one factor layer at a time. A parallel rise of one hundred basis
points costs each of the ten bond classes its duration times one percent,
between `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * rng("curves +100 bp", bond_cl)[2])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * rng("curves +100 bp", bond_cl)[1])` percent, and
moves nothing else. The minimum-variance portfolio, which holds
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * W["US_government", "minimum variance"])` percent of
`US_government`, loses
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("minimum variance", "curves +100 bp"))` percent
and is the worst of the four portfolios, against
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("equal weight", "curves +100 bp"))` for equal
weight: the least volatile portfolio of @sec-09-mean-variance-application is a
concentrated position in the one factor this scenario shocks. The spread
widening with equities down fifteen percent is the credit crisis in miniature.
Each credit class loses its spread duration times two percent, between
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * rng("spreads +200 bp, equities -15%", grep("_credit$", colnames(R), value = TRUE))[2])`
and
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * rng("spreads +200 bp, equities -15%", grep("_credit$", colnames(R), value = TRUE))[1])`
percent, every equity class its fifteen, and the ranking reverses: equal weight
loses `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("equal weight", "spreads +200 bp, equities -15%"))`
percent and minimum variance
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("minimum variance", "spreads +200 bp, equities -15%"))`.
The dollar scenario touches no US series and the commodity index and takes ten
percent from every other class, so it is a test of home bias: equal weight,
with twelve of its sixteen series abroad, loses
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("equal weight", "dollar +10%"))` percent, the
policy portfolio `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("policy", "dollar +10%"))`
and minimum variance
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("minimum variance", "dollar +10%"))`. The
sell-off with a rally is the only scenario in which the bond block gains,
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * rng("equities -25%, curves -50 bp", bond_cl)[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * rng("equities -25%, curves -50 bp", bond_cl)[2])`
percent on fifty basis points, and the
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * sum(W[grep("_equity$", rownames(W)), "policy"]))`
percent the policy portfolio holds in equity costs it
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("policy", "equities -25%, curves -50 bp"))`
percent against
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * pf_at("minimum variance", "equities -25%, curves -50 bp"))`
for minimum variance. In three of the four scenarios minimum variance loses
least and equal weight most; in the parallel rise it is the other way round.
Every number in the table is a weighted sum of a row of @tbl-965-classes, and
that is the point: a scenario return can be traced to the loading that
produced it.

What a linear one-period mapping leaves out is listed rather than hidden. It
has no convexity, so a large yield move is priced by the first-order term of
@eq-22-return alone and the loss on a rise is overstated, the gain on a fall
understated. It holds the exposures fixed, whereas @longin2001 and @ang2002
show that correlations rise in falling markets and @chow1999 build the
scenario portfolio on exactly that distinction between good and bad regimes.
It has no second round: a spread widening that forces selling, or a currency
move that changes a central bank's policy, is a path and not a vector. And it
carries no idiosyncratic draw, so an instrument's return under a scenario is
its systematic return only, which for the median equity is
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * r2_at("instrument", "equity", "median"))` percent of
its variance. The last two limits are what the turbulence measure of
@kritzman2010 and the coherent scenarios of @rebonato2010 are built to
address, and the next section measures the first and the last.

## Scenarios Against the Episodes {#sec-965-scenario-analysis-episodes}

The validation treats each episode of `sim_episodes` as a scenario the market
actually ran. The realized factor moves over an episode's weeks are the sum of
the weekly changes for the curve factors and the spreads and the compounded
return for the currencies, the equity markets and the commodity index; pushed
through $\boldsymbol{B}$, with each regression's constant times the number of
weeks added, which for a bond is mostly its carry, they give the cumulative
return the mapping predicts. The realized returns are the ones
@sec-90-data-description tables for the classes, which the chunk asserts, and
their counterparts for the instruments.

```{r}
#| label: episodes
lv <- c(lsc, grep("_Spread$", names(cv), value = TRUE))        # factors that are changes
rt <- setdiff(colnames(F), lv)                                  # factors that are returns
episode_shock <- function(e) {
  i <- which(in_episode(wk, e))
  shock(colSums(F[i, lv]), apply(1 + F[i, rt, drop = FALSE], 2, prod) - 1)
}
fit <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(sim_episodes$episode, function(e) {
  i <- which(in_episode(wk, e)); m <- in_episode(zoo::index(R), e)
  realized <- apply(1 + Y[i, ], 2, prod) - 1
  stopifnot(max(abs(realized[colnames(R)] - (apply(1 + R[m, ], 2, prod) - 1))) < 1e-8)
  tibble::tibble(episode = sim_episodes$label[sim_episodes$episode == e], name = meta$name,
                 level = meta$level, kind = meta$kind,
                 predicted = propagate(episode_shock(e), B) + alpha * length(i),
                 realized = realized[meta$name])
})) |> dplyr::mutate(episode = factor(episode, sim_episodes$label))
r2_line <- function(y, yhat) 1 - sum((y - yhat)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2)   # against the 45-degree line
fit_tab <- fit |>
  dplyr::group_by(episode) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    r2_classes     = r2_line(realized[level == "class"], predicted[level == "class"]),
    r2_instruments = r2_line(realized[level == "instrument"], predicted[level == "instrument"]),
    miss_class     = name[level == "class"][which.max(abs(realized - predicted)[level == "class"])],
    miss_instrument = name[level == "instrument"][which.max(abs(realized - predicted)[level == "instrument"])],
    .groups = "drop")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-965-fit
#| tbl-cap: "The mapping against the four episodes: the R² of predicted cumulative returns against realized ones, measured against the 45-degree line, across the sixteen classes and across the instruments, and the series each misses by most."
#| echo: false
fit_tab |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(r2_classes, r2_instruments), ~ sprintf("%.3f", .x))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrll",
        col.names = c("episode", "R², classes", "R², instruments", "largest miss, class", "largest miss, instrument"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-965-episodes
#| fig-cap: "Predicted against realized cumulative returns over the four episodes, one panel per episode, the line the 45-degree line. Small points are instruments, large ones the sixteen class series; the bonds sit on the line and the equities scatter around it."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.85
fit |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = factor(kind, c("government", "credit", "money_market", "equity", "commodity"))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(predicted, realized, colour = kind)) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink_soft"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = function(d) dplyr::filter(d, level == "instrument"), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = function(d) dplyr::filter(d, level == "class"), size = 3, shape = 17) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ episode, scales = "free") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "predicted by the mapping", y = "realized")
```

```{r}
#| label: fit-facts
#| include: false
ft <- function(e, col) fit_tab[[col]][fit_tab$episode == e]
miss <- fit |> dplyr::mutate(err = realized - predicted)
miss_at <- function(e, nm, col = "err") miss[[col]][miss$episode == e & miss$name == nm]
eq_miss <- miss |> dplyr::filter(level == "instrument", kind == "equity") |>
  dplyr::group_by(episode) |> dplyr::summarise(mad = mean(abs(err)), .groups = "drop")
bond_miss <- miss |> dplyr::filter(level == "instrument", kind %in% c("government", "credit")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(episode) |> dplyr::summarise(mad = mean(abs(err)), .groups = "drop")
gov_cl <- grep("_government$", colnames(R), value = TRUE)
conv   <- miss |> dplyr::filter(episode == "rates shock", name %in% gov_cl)
lbl    <- setNames(sim_episodes$label, sim_episodes$episode)
mad_at <- function(tab, e) tab$mad[tab$episode == e]
hy_uk  <- sapply(sim_episodes$episode, function(e) episode_shock(e)[["UK_HY_Spread"]])
y_rs0  <- cv$US_Level[min(which(in_episode(cv$date, "rates_shock"))) - 1L]   # the week before
stopifnot(names(which.max(hy_uk)) == "credit_crisis", hy_uk[["credit_crisis"]] > 0.02,
          y_rs0 < mean(cv$US_Level))
stopifnot(all(fit_tab$r2_classes > 0.95), all(fit_tab$r2_instruments < 0.7),
          all(fit_tab$r2_classes > fit_tab$r2_instruments),
          all(eq_miss$mad > bond_miss$mad),
          ft(lbl[["equity_bear"]], "miss_class") == "JP_equity",
          miss_at(lbl[["equity_bear"]], "JP_equity") > 0,
          ft(lbl[["credit_crisis"]], "miss_class") == "UK_credit",
          miss_at(lbl[["credit_crisis"]], "UK_credit") > 0,
          miss_at(lbl[["credit_crisis"]], "UK_credit", "realized") < 0,
          all(conv$err < 0),                                      # carry credited, not earned
          all(grepl("_EQU_", fit_tab$miss_instrument)),
          which.max(abs(miss$err[miss$level == "instrument"])) %in%
            which(miss$episode[miss$level == "instrument"] == lbl[["equity_bear"]]))
```

@tbl-965-fit and @fig-965-episodes give the answer. Across the sixteen
classes the mapping explains between
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * min(fit_tab$r2_classes))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * max(fit_tab$r2_classes))` percent of the variation
in cumulative returns, measured against the 45-degree line without refitting,
and the misses have names. In the
`r lbl[["equity_bear"]]` the class the mapping misses by most is `JP_equity`,
whose realized return lies
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * miss_at(lbl[["equity_bear"]], "JP_equity"))`
percentage points above the prediction over the
`r sum(in_episode(zoo::index(R), "equity_bear"))` months of the episode: a
foreign class is its local market *times* its currency and the mapping adds
them, so the longer the window and the larger the moves, the larger the cross
term it leaves out. In the `r lbl[["credit_crisis"]]` it is `UK_credit`, which
lost `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * miss_at(lbl[["credit_crisis"]], "UK_credit", "realized"))`
percent against a predicted
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * miss_at(lbl[["credit_crisis"]], "UK_credit", "predicted"))`:
the UK high-yield spread widened by
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * hy_uk[["credit_crisis"]])` basis points, the largest
move of the four episodes, and a spread duration alone overstates the loss on
a move of that size by the convexity term of @eq-22-return, which a spread has
as much as a yield. In the `r lbl[["rates_shock"]]` the five government classes
sit just below the line, by
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * mean(conv$err))` percentage points on average over
the year: the mapping credits each bond with its sample-average carry, and the
episode starts from a US level of
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * y_rs0)` percent against a sample mean of
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(cv$US_Level))`. Across the instruments
the $R^2$ falls to between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(fit_tab$r2_instruments))`
and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(fit_tab$r2_instruments))`, and the largest miss in
every episode is a single equity, by as much as
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(abs(miss$err[miss$level == "instrument"])))`
percentage points for one name over the `r lbl[["equity_bear"]]`: the
idiosyncratic draw, which carries the larger part of a single equity's
variance in @fig-965-r2 and which no scenario can reach. In that episode the
mean absolute miss of the `r r2_at("instrument", "equity", "n")` equities is
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mad_at(eq_miss, lbl[["equity_bear"]]))` percentage
points against `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mad_at(bond_miss, lbl[["equity_bear"]]))`
for the bonds. The mapping is, then, what it was said to be: exact for the
factor layers, exact for the bonds up to convexity, carry and compounding, and
silent on the draw.

The stress test of the mandate of @sec-12-constraints-application closes the
appendix. The mandate is minimum variance under seven linear lines, fully
invested, no series above 35 percent, equities between 40 and 60 percent,
government at least 10, credit at most 40, commodities at most 15 percent, and
an expected excess return of at least six percent a year, with the position
limit of eight imposed afterwards by the screen of that chapter. The lines are
added one at a time from the long-only minimum-variance portfolio of
@sec-09-mean-variance-application, so that the line that accounts for a
difference can be read off.

```{r}
#| label: mandate
grp   <- split(seq_along(colnames(Re)), sleeve_of(colnames(Re)))
m_min <- c(commodity = 0.00, credit = 0.00, equity = 0.40, government = 0.10)
m_max <- c(commodity = 0.15, credit = 0.40, equity = 0.60, government = 1.00)
stopifnot(identical(names(grp), names(m_min)), identical(names(grp), names(m_max)))
floor_ann <- 0.06
min_var <- function(spec, X = Re) {
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(X, spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                                         optimize_method = "ROI"))
  stopifnot(!anyNA(w)); w
}
lines <- function(assets, with_group = TRUE, with_floor = TRUE) {
  g <- split(seq_along(assets), sleeve_of(assets))
  s <- portfolio.spec(assets = assets) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.35)
  if (with_group) s <- s |> add.constraint(type = "group", groups = g,
                                           group_min = unname(m_min[names(g)]),
                                           group_max = unname(m_max[names(g)]))
  if (with_floor) s <- s |> add.constraint(type = "return", return_target = floor_ann / 12)
  s
}
full <- function(w) { out <- setNames(rep(0, ncol(Re)), colnames(Re)); out[names(w)] <- w; out }
w_cap   <- min_var(lines(colnames(Re), FALSE, FALSE))
w_grp   <- min_var(lines(colnames(Re), TRUE, FALSE))
w_floor <- min_var(lines(colnames(Re)))
keep    <- names(sort(w_floor, decreasing = TRUE))[1:8]            # the screen of chapter 12
w_mand  <- full(min_var(lines(keep), Re[, keep]))
W_m <- cbind(`long only` = w_gmv[colnames(Re)], `+ 35% cap` = w_cap[colnames(Re)],
             `+ class limits` = w_grp[colnames(Re)], `+ 6% floor` = w_floor[colnames(Re)],
             `+ 8 positions (the mandate)` = w_mand[colnames(Re)])
stopifnot(identical(rownames(W_m), colnames(R)), all(abs(colSums(W_m) - 1) < 1e-6),
          sum(w_mand > 1e-6) <= 8L, sum(mu * w_mand) * 12 >= floor_ann - 1e-6)
S_m <- t(W_m) %*% S_class
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-965-mandate
#| tbl-cap: "The mandate of chapter 12 under the four scenarios, one rung at a time: the long-only minimum-variance portfolio, then with each line of the policy statement added in turn. The last row is the mandate."
#| echo: false
tibble::as_tibble(S_m, rownames = "portfolio") |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-portfolio, ~ sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * .x))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: mandate-facts
#| include: false
mand_better <- S_m["+ 8 positions (the mandate)", ] > S_m["long only", ]
steps <- apply(S_m, 2, diff)                                     # the change each rung makes
rownames(steps) <- colnames(W_m)[-1]
accounts <- apply(steps, 2, function(x) rownames(steps)[which.max(abs(x))])
sm <- function(p, s) S_m[p, s]
share <- function(rung, pattern) sum(W_m[grepl(pattern, rownames(W_m)), rung])
stopifnot(identical(unname(mand_better), c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)),
          accounts[["curves +100 bp"]] == "+ class limits",
          abs(steps["+ 35% cap", "curves +100 bp"]) < 0.001,
          accounts[["spreads +200 bp, equities -15%"]] == "+ 35% cap",
          W_m["US_credit", "+ 35% cap"] > 0.2, W_m["US_credit", "long only"] < 0.001,
          accounts[["equities -25%, curves -50 bp"]] == "+ class limits",
          accounts[["dollar +10%"]] == "+ 6% floor", steps["+ 6% floor", "dollar +10%"] > 0,
          share("+ class limits", "_(government|credit)$") < share("+ 35% cap", "_(government|credit)$"),
          share("+ class limits", "_equity$") >= 0.40 - 1e-6,
          W_m["US_equity", "+ 6% floor"] > W_m["US_equity", "+ class limits"],
          share("+ 6% floor", "^(UK|EU|CH|JP)_") < share("+ class limits", "^(UK|EU|CH|JP)_"))
```

@tbl-965-mandate answers the question the mandate was written for. In one of
the four scenarios the mandate loses less than the long-only minimum-variance
portfolio: the parallel rise,
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * sm("+ 8 positions (the mandate)", "curves +100 bp"))`
against `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * sm("long only", "curves +100 bp"))`
percent, and the rung that accounts for it is the class limits. The cap alone
changes nothing in that scenario, because the weight it releases from
`US_government` goes to other bonds of the same duration; the class limits
require forty percent in equities and so cut the bond block from
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * share("+ 35% cap", "_(government|credit)$"))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * share("+ class limits", "_(government|credit)$"))`
percent of the portfolio, and with it the duration. The same lines are what
make the mandate lose more in the other three. In the spread widening the cap
is the largest step, from
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * sm("long only", "spreads +200 bp, equities -15%"))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * sm("+ 35% cap", "spreads +200 bp, equities -15%"))`
percent, because the weight it releases goes in part to `US_credit`,
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * W_m["US_credit", "+ 35% cap"])` percent of the
portfolio at that rung against none before, which carries the spread duration
the scenario shocks. In the sell-off the class limits are, taking the loss
from `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * sm("+ 35% cap", "equities -25%, curves -50 bp"))`
to `r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * sm("+ class limits", "equities -25%, curves -50 bp"))`
percent, which is what a forty percent equity floor means in a sell-off of
twenty-five percent. And in the dollar scenario the return floor runs the
other way, reducing the loss by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * steps["+ 6% floor", "dollar +10%"])` percentage
points, because the expected return it demands is bought with `US_equity`,
which rises from
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * W_m["US_equity", "+ class limits"])` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * W_m["US_equity", "+ 6% floor"])` percent at the
expense of the foreign series the scenario hits. A mandate is a set of
exposures the committee has chosen without naming them, and the table names
them: the equity floor is a duration ceiling and a sell-off exposure, the cap
is a decision to hold the spread duration the minimum-variance portfolio would
not, and the return floor is a dollar position.

That is what a reader can do with this appendix. A scenario is a vector,
`shock()` names its entries, $\boldsymbol{B}$ carries one row per instrument
and per class, and `propagate()` is one matrix product: any scenario a
committee can write as factor moves, any portfolio written as weights by name,
and any exposure matrix, the regression betas of
@sec-05-factor-models-implementation or the durations of
@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-implementation, can be substituted in a line. The
book's data make both sides inspectable, and the four episodes say how far to
trust the result: to within a few percentage points for the factor layers and
the bonds, and not at all for the draw.
